# NATS message plane foundation

Status: design, campaign ct_00000000-0000-400c-98d7-22df1cf499d8 (2026-09-18). Nothing below is shipped yet; the slices implement it.

Source: owner-loop-round-4.md of campaign ct_00000000-0000-400c-98d7-22df1cf499d8, extracted verbatim. This is the normative text every slice implements; the root draft in drafts/ is the pre-review sketch.


## intent

Stand up the fourth CortexKit plane the Takim PRD reserved ("all async agent communication on embedded NATS") and subconscious's design handoff scheduled as phase 4, so that agent-to-agent traffic stops being carried by the tool wire plus per-module SQLite outboxes. Today rooms, wakes, peer deliveries, ask answers and Pi plugin-session pushes each reinvent a delivery mechanism per harness (prefrontal's `agent_delivery`, `wake_fire`, `effect_intent`; the daemon's push-hint egress; a directory-keyed provider probe that missed a chair on 2026-09-18 after a module restart). This foundation defines the plane once: topology, names and grants, primitives, identity, credentials, census, federation and tenancy. It ports nothing yet; the ports are later slices that delete the per-harness mechanics one at a time.

Citation form. Two rooms decide everything below, and every ruling resolves to a post. Bare `#N` and `room #N` mean post N in `nats-plane: message bus foundation` (rm_toolu_01Rr9P2WQ194VqWc13bvLYLT), with SUBC and CALLO. `federation #N` means post N in `federation-sync` (rm_toolu_01JLnS2zCSpf96mZaJ5GSLgJ), with CKCRED. Operator rulings additionally carry their ask id (for example ask_3259e52a). A citation without one of these two forms is not a ruling and does not bind a slice.

Evidence pinning. In-repo citations are pinned at de2e5f1c6ad6 (HEAD is c8114751f312; none of the cited files changed between the two). These cross-repo citations are **unverified by this package** and carry no commit pin: `PRD.md:136-158`, `subconscious-design-handoff.md` section 3.3, subconscious `supervise.rs:4685-4714` and the 30 s drain ceiling attributed to it, the daemon's push-hint egress depth, and the `ck module terminals nats` surface. Consequence, not decoration: no acceptance control may hard-code a constant taken from an unverified citation. The drain-ceiling control reads the supervisor's declared value at run time (constraints, Topology), and the egress depth is quoted as motivation only, never as a threshold.

Terms used throughout. SUBC — the subconscious seat, owner of the daemon, supervisor and `subc.jsonc`. CALLO — the Callosum seat, owner of federation, the roster and the pairing ceremony. CKCRED — the Claustrum-credential seat, owner of vault signing records and `credential.sign`. CKIOS — the iOS seat, owner of shipped phone builds and the fed-wire hello decoder there. RelayDO — Callosum's Cloudflare Durable Object relay, considered here only as a possible leaf tunnel. bit-7 census — the 2026-09-18 sweep that established which running binaries understood protocol bit 7, possible only because the daemon registry saw every module at HELLO. aft#277 class — the defect class in which secret material reachable from a process's environment is inherited by a child process. "missed a chair" — the 2026-09-18 incident in which a directory-keyed provider probe reported an agent seat in a room absent after an unrelated module restart. phase 4b — the later phase that would add a hubless topology, if one turns out to exist.


## constraints

Topology.
- `nats-server` (Go) runs as a subc-supervised sibling process. The daemon neither speaks NATS nor holds a NATS credential nor has a Claustrum route. Modules connect with `async-nats` through a thin NATS-shaped trait layer (Stream, Register, WorkQueue) whose only second backend is in-memory for tests; portability across queue services is not a design input (operator ruling, room #10). Never bend the stream or register primitives to fit a backend list.
- Prerequisite on SUBC's plane (rooms #8, #15, #19): a declared per-module `protocol: "none"` mode that switches teardown to SIGTERM, wait, SIGKILL; suppresses health probing; and reads `live` as not-applicable. It must be declared, never inferred from "has not registered yet". Without it every restart SIGKILLs JetStream after the supervisor's drain ceiling (subconscious `supervise.rs:4685-4714`, unverified at this package's pin — the acceptance control reads the ceiling from the supervisor's declared configuration at run time and never hard-codes 30 s). That mode tells the daemon only that the process exists, and it keeps the process-level restart budget and escalating backoff, so a crash-looping server stops at the budget instead of spinning; that retained supervision is why the server runs under subc rather than outside it. Bus health is the sentinel probe's job (below), not the supervisor's.
- Boot ordering (room #19): `subc.jsonc` orders nothing; modules spawn concurrently and a participant may connect before the server listens. Participants treat the server as absent-then-arriving, never present-at-start. No spawn ordering is added: a promise the supervisor cannot keep across a 03:00 crash is not a promise. The cold-start herd is sized here (Constants), not deferred to a later slice — this is the topology cut.
- The tool wire stays as it is (rooms #8, #7): request/response with a daemon-stamped principal, body forwarded untouched, hot-swap supervision. NATS request/reply never takes over module-to-module calls.
- The bus never rides Callosum's fed-wire (room #7: fed-wire is request/response only, subscriptions refused at origin by a pinned gate). Cross-host is a NATS leaf connection on its own TCP. The leaf learns where the hub is from Callosum, never by re-deriving addresses, through a new local management op on CALLO's plane (room #20; working name `callosum.hub_read`): for the peer the roster marks as hub, its pinned identity (see Trust anchors) plus its current candidate addresses in dial order, refused to federated callers like the existing three ops. The leaf re-reads it on every reconnect and on the poll period in Constants; an absent hub identity (roster row tombstoned) means disconnect, and a changed hub identity is noticed on the same read, so one op answers both and the link never outlives the pairing (room #24). RelayDO as a leaf tunnel only if a hubless topology actually exists (phase 4b).
- Leaf-side signing is an unresolved prerequisite, stated rather than assumed. Stock `nats-server` reads its outbound leaf credential from a creds file, i.e. a seed on disk, which this spec forbids; it has no hook that would let it call `credential.sign`. Three candidate shapes, decision owed by SUBC and CKCRED before the link arm becomes a gate: (i) the leaf link is carried by a Rust bridge process holding an `async-nats` connection to each side, paying a message copy and a second hop; (ii) the bus module hands the server an unlinked memory-backed creds fd at spawn — a bounded, written-down exception to "no seed in a file" that must name its own hazard; (iii) upstream support for an external signer callback. Until one is chosen, the link arm runs under a labelled shape and does not claim seedless leaf authentication.
- Sentinel probe (the plane's health component; "arm" is reserved for acceptance arms). It is hosted by the bus module process, not by the supervisor and not by a participant, and that process is both requester and responder: one task publishes a request on `ck.{acct}.sentinel.ping` carrying a reply subject under its own `_INBOX.{credential_public}` prefix, and a second subscription in the same process answers by publishing to that reply subject, so the round trip traverses the server and the probe measures the server rather than the process. The answer is an inbox *publish*, which is why the bus-module grant below carries publish as well as subscribe on `_INBOX.{credential_public}.>`: without it the responder is refused and the probe reports down forever against a healthy server. No participant holds any sentinel grant, publish or subscribe. Period 10 s, timeout 2 s; three consecutive failures or timeouts report `bus.health.down` with the last error's taxonomy class, and the first success after a down reports `bus.health.up`. Class attribution is stated rather than left to the implementation, because one failure has two observables: the requester's own observable is a reply timeout, whose class is `Unavailable`, while a responder refused on its own reply publish surfaces a server permissions violation asynchronously on the connection's error handler and never as a return from `publish`. The probe therefore registers that async-error surface, and a permissions violation for its own sentinel or inbox subjects observed within the same probe period sets the reported class to `Denied` in preference to the requester's timeout class; with no such violation the class is the requester's. A8 separates the two by observation — reply publish permitted with the server stopped reports `Unavailable`, reply publish removed against a healthy server reports `Denied` — so the rule is falsifiable rather than a naming convention. Before the server has ever answered — the absent-then-arriving case — the probe reports `bus.health.down` with class `Unavailable`; it never reports healthy from silence. The verdict is read by `ck` as the plane's health surface and by nothing that gates spawning. A sentinel that cannot mint or hold its own credential reports down rather than absent.

Names and grants. Every name below is derivable from registry identity, account and room membership alone, so later port slices and server permission files can be generated rather than negotiated.
- Account token `{acct}`: the account slug carried on the credential's account field. On a box that has never paired it is `box_<roster_host_id>`. Stability is normative: `{acct}` is fixed for the life of the box. Pairing links the box account to a hub; it never renames it, because every stream, bucket and durable cursor embeds the token and a rename is a data migration rather than a config change. If CALLO's ceremony cannot hold that, it is a spec edit that must carry the migration for streams and durable consumers, and every A4 durability claim is scoped to one side of that boundary until it does.
- Account uppercasing is injective, which the earlier `-`-to-`_` mapping was not (`box_a-b` and `box_a_b` both produced `BOX_A_B`, silently merging two accounts' streams and buckets). `{acct}` therefore matches a narrower lexicon than the other tokens: `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_]{0,62}`, no hyphen. `{ACCT}` is `{acct}` uppercased ASCII and nothing else. A `<roster_host_id>` containing a hyphen or any other out-of-lexicon byte is refused at account derivation with the offending token named — never mapped — and the naming crate's tests cover exactly the pair above: `box_a-b` refused, `box_a_b` accepted.
- Naming rule and its closed exemption list. The token rule binds every `ck.`-rooted subject, every stream name and every bucket name; the naming crate's test fails the build on any of those that omits the token. Exempt, asserted by enumeration in the same test so the list cannot quietly grow: the NATS-owned prefixes `_INBOX.`, `$JS.`, `$KV.`, `$SYS.` — namespaces this spec does not get to rename — and durable consumer names, which are scoped by the stream they live on and whose stream name already carries the token. `c_{agent_id}` is therefore the normative workload consumer name, and the same agent id under two accounts is two consumers on two streams; `c_ckbus_dead` on `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD` is the single module-owned durable and falls under the same exemption.
- Token lexicon. Every interpolated token other than `{acct}` (`{agent_id}`, `{session_id}`, `{room_id}`, `{module_id}`, `<roster_host_id>`) matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,62}`: no dot, no `*`, no `>`, no whitespace, 63 bytes maximum. There is no `{workload}` token; subject families are enumerated literally below. A token outside the lexicon is refused at the call site with the offending token named and is never silently normalized, because normalization is how two identities become one. Session and room ids reach this plane as host-supplied free text — at the pinned snapshot the peer store carries `peer_messages.from_session_id` and `peer_messages.to_session_id` (`crates/prefrontal-core-store/migrations/002_peer_messages.sql:26-45`) and `peers.session_id`, all `TEXT` with no format constraint — so the port slice that carries a workload is the slice that proves its ids are in the lexicon or maps them in its own store; this cut ships the refusal and the per-rule naming test, not the mapping. `<roster_host_id>`'s lexical form is CALLO's to define; this spec requires the form above, plus the hyphen-free account narrowing when it is used to derive `{acct}`, and the pairing arm fails if what arrives does not meet it.
- Subjects: room post `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.post`; wake `ck.{acct}.wake.{agent_id}.fire`; peer delivery `ck.{acct}.peer.{agent_id}.{session_id}.deliver`; effect intent `ck.{acct}.effect.{agent_id}.{session_id}.intent`; effect dead letter `ck.{acct}.effect.dead`; sentinel probe `ck.{acct}.sentinel.ping`. Tokens are registry ids only — never a directory path, a device key, a credential public key or a spawn generation.
- Consumer filter subjects are narrower than the subscribe grants, and the two are stated separately because the server applies different checks to them: a grant is matched per message, while a consumer's filter subject must be a *subset* of its stream's binding or the create is refused with `JSConsumerFilterNotSubsetErr`. A room consumer therefore filters on the literal `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.post`, one entry per bound room in `filter_subjects`; a peer consumer on `ck.{acct}.peer.{agent_id}.*.deliver`; a wake consumer on `ck.{acct}.wake.{agent_id}.fire`; an effect consumer on `ck.{acct}.effect.{agent_id}.*.intent`; `c_ckbus_dead` on the literal `ck.{acct}.effect.dead`. The wider `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.>` and `ck.{acct}.peer.{agent_id}.>` forms are subscribe grants only and are never used as filter subjects — against these bindings a trailing `>` filter is refused at create on every one of these streams, which is the failure the limits crate reproduces before the server is asked.
- Streams, five and named literally everywhere they appear: `CK_{ACCT}_ROOM`, `CK_{ACCT}_WAKE`, `CK_{ACCT}_PEER`, the work-queue `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT`, and the dead-letter `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD`, each with the limits in Constants. Every grant, permission emission and bootstrap step below enumerates all five; the bus module creates and manages all five, because a dead-letter stream the bus module cannot create makes terminal disposition unexecutable on a fresh box. Durable workload consumer name is `c_{agent_id}`, derived from registry identity alone, so a respawn or a device re-key never changes it. Those consumers have a named creator: the bus module creates them under its management grant at the moment it mints a participant's credential — one per bound stream, with the filter subjects above and the configuration in Constants — because the per-process grant carries pull, ack and INFO but no create, and a consumer nobody is allowed to create is a consumer that does not exist. A membership change re-mints and adjusts the room consumer's `filter_subjects` in the same act. The rig's F-PROV fixture stands in for this while the bus module is unlanded (acceptance_sketch).
- Stream subject bindings, literal and pairwise disjoint, because a subject captured by two streams is refused by the server at stream create and would fail install bootstrap step (5) on a fresh box, and because a work queue that captured its own dead letter would re-enqueue everything it just terminated. `CK_{ACCT}_ROOM` binds `ck.{acct}.room.*.post`; `CK_{ACCT}_WAKE` binds `ck.{acct}.wake.*.fire`; `CK_{ACCT}_PEER` binds `ck.{acct}.peer.*.*.deliver`; `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT` binds `ck.{acct}.effect.*.*.intent` and never the wider `ck.{acct}.effect.>`; `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD` binds the literal `ck.{acct}.effect.dead`. `ck.{acct}.sentinel.ping` is bound by no stream: the probe is request/reply and is never persisted. These bindings are what make the consumer filter forms above mandatory rather than stylistic. The naming-and-limits crate refuses any configuration in which two stream filters overlap, refuses a work-queue stream whose filter overlaps any other stream's, and refuses a consumer whose filter subject is not a subset of its stream's binding — all before the server ever sees it; the terminal-disposition and stream-binding arms carry the matching controls.
- Census bucket `CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS` (backing stream `KV_CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS`), key `{module_id}`, history 1, no TTL (Census, below). Value: `{credential_public, user_jwt_id, spawn_generation, credential_epoch, schema_versions, identities, rooms}`. The `user_jwt_id` is there because revocation step (1) needs it and the bus module reads it out of the value it is about to delete. One key per live module process; a respawn overwrites the same key with a new credential public at a higher spawn generation and epoch 0, and a membership re-mint overwrites it at the same generation and the next epoch, which is what bounds bucket growth across a crash loop.
- Spawn generation and credential epoch are two counters and never one, because a membership change rotates a credential without a respawn. `{generation}` is SUBC's spawn generation for that module process, visible in the spawn snapshot; the bus module never allocates it. `{epoch}` is a credential counter owned by the bus module, starting at 0 for each new generation and incremented by every re-mint that is not a respawn (room membership change, planned rotation). Record names, census values and grants carry both, and authority is the lexicographic order of (generation, epoch): a connect or a mint below the highest pair the bus module has issued for that module is refused. Fencing against the spawn snapshot compares generations only — a mint for generation N is refused when the snapshot shows a higher generation, and an epoch bump against the snapshot's current generation is not a stale mint. Collapsing the two would write a census generation the supervisor's snapshot contradicts and would collide with the record name the next real respawn needs.
- Credential record names, so CKCRED and the port slices mint against a grammar rather than an example: per-process `nats.{module_id}.g{generation}.e{epoch}`; bus module's own `nats.ckbus.g{generation}.e{epoch}`; per-host leaf `nats.leaf.{roster_host_id}`; box-local operator signing key `nats.operator.{acct}`; box account signing key `nats.account.{acct}`; system account signing key `nats.sysaccount.{acct}`. These are the record-name values the arms read out of Claustrum's audit log.
- Inbox prefix is normative client configuration, not a library default. Every client on this plane sets its inbox prefix to `_INBOX.{credential_public}` before connecting, so the generated subscribe grant and the actual reply subject agree; `async-nats`'s default random `_INBOX.<nuid>` prefix produces a subscribe the grant does not cover, which denies every request/reply on this plane including the KV direct get and the watch snapshot. The enforcement boundary is subscribe, not connect, and the spec says so because an arm expecting a connect refusal fails a correct server: a client holding a valid JWT with the default prefix *connects*, and the server refuses its reply subscription with a permissions violation, which the trait layer maps to `Denied` and which makes every request on that connection time out. A8 and A9 exercise it at exactly that boundary.
- Permission files are allow-only, and this is a correctness rule rather than a style: in NATS a `deny` entry wins over an `allow`, so "allow these three API subjects, deny all other `$JS.API.>`" denies the three as well. Denial here is by omission from the allow list and the generator emits no `deny` entry. Wildcards are whole-token only, so `CK_{ACCT}_*` is a literal string containing an asterisk and matches nothing; every stream-bearing subject is emitted with the five literal stream names expanded per account.
- Grant template, per-process credential. It is minted from the (module id, spawn generation, credential epoch, bound agent ids, bound room ids) tuple recorded in the census value, and it enumerates subjects — no `{workload}` or bare `{identity}` placeholder survives into an emitted file. Publish, per bound agent id: `ck.{acct}.wake.{agent_id}.fire`, `ck.{acct}.peer.{agent_id}.>`, `ck.{acct}.effect.{agent_id}.>`; per bound room id: `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.post`; plus `ck.{acct}.effect.dead` (terminal disposition, below). No sentinel grant of any kind. Subscribe: `_INBOX.{credential_public}.>`, `ck.{acct}.peer.{agent_id}.>` per bound agent id, `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.>` per bound room id — these are grants, matched per message, and are deliberately wider than the consumer filter subjects above. Ack, literal per stream and never `$JS.ACK.>` or a partial-token wildcard, because an unscoped ack grant lets one identity ack or term another identity's delivery: `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_ROOM.c_{agent_id}.>`, `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_WAKE.c_{agent_id}.>`, `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_PEER.c_{agent_id}.>`, `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT.c_{agent_id}.>`. JetStream API, literal per stream: `$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.CK_{ACCT}_{ROOM|WAKE|PEER|EFFECT}.c_{agent_id}`, `$JS.API.CONSUMER.INFO.<same>.c_{agent_id}`, `$JS.API.STREAM.INFO.<same>`. No consumer create on any of the four workload streams; the bus module creates them (Streams, above). Census read: subscribe `$KV.CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS.>` plus the request subjects a KV get and a KV watch actually issue against `KV_CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS` — direct get, stream info, and ordered-consumer create and delete under that stream name — because a `$KV` subscribe permission alone does not authorize the JetStream requests a snapshot needs, and because an ordered watch *is* a consumer create the participant must be allowed to make there and nowhere else. The exact request set is not copied from documentation: arm A9 enumerates it against a running server and the permission generator's golden is that arm's committed output.
- Room membership is mutable, so its grant has a stated lifecycle rather than an assumed one. A credential carries the room set of the moment it was minted; a membership change is executed as a re-mint at the next credential epoch of the same spawn generation, followed by a client reconnect under the new credential, with the census key overwritten at that (generation, epoch) and the room consumer's `filter_subjects` adjusted by the same act, and it takes effect within the membership re-mint bound in Constants. The superseded epoch is revoked by the four steps below, so a membership change that removes a room is enforced by the server and not by the client's good manners. A participant publishing to a room it is not bound to is refused by the server (`Denied`), which is the property A9 exercises in both directions across a membership change. The plane does not grant `ck.{acct}.room.>` to keep a rename or a join cheap.
- Grant template, bus module credential (box account). Census read *and* write, because a write-only census grant makes the reconciliation sweep and revocation unexecutable: subscribe and write on `$KV.CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS.>`, plus the KV API subjects for get, put, delete, direct get, stream info and ordered-consumer create and delete on `KV_CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS` — the sweep reads every key to find entries with no live generation, and revocation step (1) reads `user_jwt_id` out of the value it is about to delete. Stream and consumer management on the five literal stream names, which is the grant under which the participants' `c_{agent_id}` durables are created. The durable `c_ckbus_dead` on `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD` with its literal ack and pull subjects (this is how the dead-letter stream gets a consumer that deduplicates on message id). Publish and subscribe on `ck.{acct}.sentinel.ping`, and publish *and* subscribe on `_INBOX.{credential_public}.>` under the same inbox-prefix rule, the publish being how the sentinel responder answers its own requester. No publish rights on any workload subject: the bus module manages the plane and never carries a workload message.
- Grant template, bus module system-account user. `$SYS` is a separate account and no box-account user can reach it, so the two server-side acts the census invariant depends on — the kick and the account claims update that carries the revocation list — have their own issuer: a system account per box, whose signing key is the Claustrum signing record `nats.sysaccount.{acct}` on that box, its JWT signed by that box's own operator key (Install bootstrap), and a second user JWT under it held only by the bus module. Its grant is exactly three things: the client-kick request subject, the `$SYS` client-connect/disconnect event subjects, and the account claims-update request subject the resolver requires (`$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.UPDATE` in 2.10, pinned by arm A9 against the running server rather than asserted here) — nothing else. If that user is absent or unmintable the bus module refuses to start and the sentinel probe reports `bus.health.down` with reason `sysaccount-absent`: revocation is never left silently unenforced.
- Grant template, per-host (leaf) credential: issued by the hub's account, scoped to `ck.{acct}.>` for the accounts linked at pairing, never including census write or system-account rights. No process credential ever crosses a host.

Primitives and the trait contract (rooms #4, #8). Two implementations may claim conformance only against this operation list and this parity table.
- Stream: `publish(subject, id, digest, headers) -> ack{stream_seq}`; `consumer(durable, identity) -> cursor`; `next()`, `ack()`, `nak(delay)`; replay from a stored cursor position. The trait binds to an existing durable rather than creating one on the workload streams, because creation is the bus module's act and the per-process grant refuses it.
- Register: `put(key, value) -> revision`; `get(key) -> Value{revision} | Absent`; `delete(key) -> tombstone`; `watch(prefix)` delivers an initial snapshot, then updates, and says which is which, and says whether the current watch has received a snapshot at all on this connection.
- WorkQueue: `claim() -> item{delivery_count}`, `ack`, `nak(delay)`, redelivery cap; on cap exhaustion the item is terminally disposed to `ck.{acct}.effect.dead` and the consumer observes `MaxDeliveriesExceeded` — exhaustion is never a silent drop.
- Terminal disposition has a named executor, because JetStream's `MaxDeliver` stops redelivery and publishes nothing. The claiming module executes it under its own credential: on observing the cap it publishes the dead-letter record (original subject, message id, digest, delivery count, reason) to `ck.{acct}.effect.dead`, and only then calls `term()` on the original. That order is normative and the crash window is stated rather than hidden: a crash between the two leaves the item redeliverable and the dead-letter record present, so `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD` is consumed by the bus module's `c_ckbus_dead` and deduplicated on message id there, and no ordering exists in which the item is both terminated and unrecorded. The dead-letter subject is outside the work queue's binding (Stream subject bindings), so the record never re-enters the queue it terminated. The bus module does not publish to `ck.{acct}.effect.dead`, because it holds no workload publish rights.
- Error taxonomy, identical on both backends: `Unavailable` (transport, or a resource limit that refuses the request — the exhausted limit is named in the report, which is why a publish refused by a full work queue is `Unavailable` and not a fifth class); `Denied` (authorization); `Absent` (no such key/body/credential record); `Clamped` (request reduced or admitted late, with the clamp and any retry-after reported). Mapping rule at the connection boundary, since one event can look like either: a connection the server closed where reauthentication is then refused maps to `Denied`; a connection lost with no refusal on the following attempt maps to `Unavailable`; a write on an already-severed socket is `Unavailable` and never `Denied`. Asynchronous permissions violations are part of this taxonomy and not a side channel: the server reports a refused subscribe or publish on the connection's error surface rather than as a return from the call, so the trait layer exposes those events as `Denied` with the offending subject named, which is what lets the sentinel attribution rule above prefer them over a requester's timeout. A `credential.sign` against a deleted or never-minted signing record is `Absent` and is a *local* failure — it is never reported as `Denied`, because the server never saw the attempt, and that distinction is what lets an arm tell client-side breakage from server-side revocation.
- Parity table. Both backends: publish ack with monotonic sequence; consumer replay within a process lifetime; register revision, absent-vs-empty, watch snapshot-then-updates; work redelivery count, cap exhaustion and dead-letter record; a publish refused by a full work queue reported `Unavailable` with the exhausted limit named, which the in-memory backend reproduces from a configured max-bytes; the error taxonomy. NATS only: cursor survives a process restart; cursor survives credential rotation and device re-key; server-enforced grant denial; reconnect refusal after revocation; asynchronous permissions-violation reporting and the sentinel class-attribution rule; leaf behaviour; `$SYS` events. Documented divergences of the in-memory backend: it loses all state on drop, has no leaf, and returns `Denied` only for fixtures that configure it. A conformance run names which set it executed; a NATS-only property asserted against the in-memory backend is a suite bug.
- The broker carries deliveries, never state of record: a message is an id plus a SHA-256 content digest in lowercase hex, and the consumer resolves the body against the owning module's store or a read op. Retention ordering is a requirement with both sides now numbered: the owning store's retention must be greater than or equal to the stream's max-age for that workload (Constants), because a stream that outlives the body produces permanently unresolvable deliveries. The comparison is executed, not assumed — the naming-and-limits crate refuses a stream configuration whose max-age exceeds the retention the port slice declares for that workload's store. A body that is absent on replay is reported `Absent`, naked, and on cap exhaustion terminally disposed with reason `body_absent`; it is never acked as delivered. A digest mismatch is quarantined and reported, never delivered. Port slices whose current records carry the body inline (`DeliveryRecord.text`, `wake_fire.user_prose`, `machine_value_json`) either satisfy the retention ordering or carry the body inline on the bus and say so in that slice.

Identity (rooms #7, #13).
- Subjects are keyed on registry agent and session identity, never on a directory, a device key or a credential. A device re-key on Callosum is a new device and must orphan nothing.
- Durable consumer cursors key on registry identity and survive a process restart and a device re-key. Nothing durable keys on either credential, on a spawn generation or on a credential epoch.

Credentials (federation #20, rooms #13, #16).
- A NATS credential is an Ed25519 nkey, which is Claustrum's SigningKey kind. Every seed is minted in its own vault and never leaves vault memory: no seed in a file, an env var, or a client process. Clients sign the server's connection nonce through `credential.sign` over their ordinary local route. Encodings (hex public key to U-prefixed base32 with CRC; raw 64-byte signature) are client-side.
- CKCRED surface this plane consumes, named because four of the six calls are unverified at this package's pin and every arm and bootstrap step that needs them must say so. Verified present: `credential_sign`, `credential_public_key`, `credential_get`/`get_scoped`, `credential_status` (`crates/prefrontal-ckcred-client/src/lib.rs:383-466, 650-691, 1028-1049` at de2e5f1c6ad6). Required and **not shown by this package**: (a) mint/create of a signing record under a caller-supplied record name and account field; (b) durable delete of a signing record; (c) an audit-log read returning record-name and caller-principal fields; (d) a box-wide admission limiter on `credential.sign` for this plane's records, refusing nothing but admitting late and reporting `Clamped` with a retry-after (Constants, cold-start herd). Names and shapes are CKCRED's to define; this spec requires their existence, their refusal errors and, for (d), the sliding-window rule stated in Constants. Every dependent arm carries the skip reasons `ckcred-mint-unlanded`, `ckcred-delete-unlanded`, `ckcred-audit-read-unlanded`, `ckcred-admission-limit-unlanded` (acceptance_sketch) and the rig fails rather than passing when one is absent.
- Per-process credential: a signing record in Claustrum keyed on (module id, spawn generation, credential epoch), rotated on respawn and on a room-membership change, presented only to the server on its own box. It is minted by the bus module, not by the supervisor (room #19): the daemon holds no credentials and has no Claustrum route, and putting a vault round-trip inside `spawn_child` would make Claustrum a boot-critical dependency and put another module's latency on the restart hot path. With the bus module holding the plane's credential and talking to Claustrum, a bus outage leaves spawning intact and the bus unavailable — the correct blast radius. A leaked process credential can at most publish as another module on its own box; the hub side never sees or trusts one, so it cannot impersonate fleet-wide (room #17).
- Child-process authentication is an open hazard, downgraded from the draft's claim. Seed absence removes seed exfiltration and nothing more. `credential.sign` is handle-less and authorized by the launch-nonce principal against the grant table's sign authority, addressed by credential *name* (`crates/prefrontal-ckcred-client/src/lib.rs:1028-1040` at de2e5f1c6ad6); a child that inherits its parent's env inherits that nonce and therefore that principal. So this spec does **not** claim a child cannot authenticate, and does not claim the aft#277 class is removed — only that the seed class is. Denying the child requires a mechanism this repository cannot supply: a distinct per-process principal stamped at spawn, or a grant keyed on (module id, spawn generation, credential epoch) with values the child cannot forge, or a per-process nonce that is not inherited. Owed by SUBC and CKCRED, with the refusal error named. Until then the child arm is a recorded observation, not a gate.
- Per-host credential: a signing record minted at the pairing ceremony as a second-plane consequence of the same human act, living as long as the roster row, dying with its tombstone; keys the leaf link host-to-hub. Never the device's Ed25519 companion key.
- User JWTs are public material carried as metadata on the signing record, not deposits; propose/promote is for secret material crossing hosts, which never happens on this plane.
- JWT chain and issuers (federation #20, room #17; shape owed confirmation by CKCRED). Decentralized auth requires a trust root in the server's own configuration, so each box has one and it is local: a **box-local operator signing key** `nats.operator.{acct}`, a Claustrum signing record under single custody in that box's vault, which signs that box's two account JWTs and nothing else. It is not the fleet operator key. The fleet operator signing key exists once, on the hub host, and signs hub-account and leaf material; it is never present on an unpaired box and none is fabricated there. Each box's account signing key is a Claustrum signing record on that box, plus the system account above; the bus module issues per-process user JWTs under that box account, so local minting never depends on the hub and a disconnected box keeps delivering. The hub's resolver trusts the fleet operator and the accounts it issued, and nothing signed by any box-local operator, so a local per-process user JWT is accepted by the local server and refused by the hub — that asymmetry is the containment, and it is testable.
- Install bootstrap, ordered, because an empty vault has no key to start from and a never-paired box has no hub to ask. Owner: SUBC's installer calling CKCRED; no step imports a pre-provisioned key; every mint step depends on the CKCRED mint op above. (1) Mint the box-local operator signing key `nats.operator.{acct}`, where `{acct}` is `box_<roster_host_id>` under the account lexicon. (2) Mint the box account signing key `nats.account.{acct}`. (3) Mint the system account signing key `nats.sysaccount.{acct}`. (4) Sign both account JWTs with the box-local operator key and write the server config (operator JWT plus resolver, below), the resolver directory, and the TLS material for the local listener, whose SPKI the local clients pin by reading it from the same install output rather than by trusting a CA. (5) The bus module starts, mints its own credential and the system-account user under those accounts, and creates the census bucket and all five streams with their literal subject bindings if absent; participant durables are created later, per participant, at credential mint time (Streams). Pairing later adds the fleet-operator-signed hub account material and the leaf configuration; it re-issues nothing already in place, does not replace the box-local operator for local users, and does not rename `{acct}`. Acceptance runs this path from an empty vault to an authenticated local publish *and* a successful `$SYS` kick with no fleet operator key anywhere in the vault.
- Resolver mode is pinned, because revocation's durability depends on it. The local server runs the directory-backed account resolver with deletion disabled: account JWT updates arrive as a claims-update request from the system-account user, are written to the resolver directory on disk, and are therefore still in force after a server restart. A memory resolver is not used on a box that must revoke, because an in-memory account update is lost on restart and would make "stays refused across a restart" false. The client presents its user JWT and a signature over the server's nonce; the server verifies the chain against the account and operator keys it resolves; the client's only trust is TLS to the server. No resolver mode asks the leaf to trust the account key. If a future resolver shape required a leaf-side account pin, it would be a roster column written by ceremony, never a vault deposit.
- Trust anchors (operator ruling, adopted 2026-09-18 21:10Z on ask_3259e52a). The LAN hub is pinned by one new roster column written only by the pairing ceremony's code-compare (CALLO, federation #19). The pin's type is the hub's TLS SPKI SHA-256, base64 — a nonce signature authenticates the *client*, so only a server-authenticating value can pin a server. Candidate addresses from `callosum.hub_read` are advisory; the pin is the authority, and a dial to any candidate address whose presented SPKI does not match the pinned value is refused before any credential is sent. The hosted hub is anchored instead by WebPKI TLS to our hostname; the server verifies the leaf's JWT and the leaf never verifies the account key. No machine holds a third CA. A pin that arrives by any path other than a ceremony is refused by roster and vault alike. Precondition of the column (room #20): the hub must present its identity inside the authenticated pairing session, a new optional field in the fed-wire hello — a frozen wire with a strict third-party decoder. Measured by CALLO (room #23): CKIOS's hello walker reads named keys by subscript and never compares the key set, so an unknown top-level field decodes on every shipped phone build today, by omission rather than policy; SUBC pinned this in the decoder's own repo (subconscious 42a7a152, FedHelloUnknownFieldTests: baseline control, stray string field, stray nested-object field, all decode), with the stated limit that it measures master, not a shipped build, which CKIOS answers for. Order: fed-wire r6.x adds the optional field, then Callosum emits — producer last, no phone build on the critical path.

Census (rooms #8, #12, #15).
- The daemon-as-registry at HELLO is what made the bit-7 census possible; NATS ignores unknown headers, so frame refusals vanish and schema drift becomes silent one layer up. Therefore a KV register of schema versions, one key per live module process, written by the **bus module under its own NATS credential** at the same moment it mints that process's credential, so joining and being censused are one act and a participant never holds write permission on its own census entry (the same property as the roster column the ceremony writes and the peer never can, room #17). The supervisor writes nothing here and holds no credential; any text implying otherwise is retracted.
- Bootstrap: the bus module mints its own credential from the box account signing key and creates the bucket and all five streams if absent; its own census key is self-written, the single named exception, and its authority rests on the box account grant rather than on a prior entry. Acceptance runs on an empty vault and empty broker store, not only on a pre-provisioned fixture; a rig fixture that mints credentials without writing their census keys is a fixture defect, because the trait layer's confirmed-absence rule would deny those publishes locally (acceptance_sketch, F-PROV).
- The bucket has no TTL. A max-age would reap the entry of a process that merely ran a long time, and by this section's own invariant that reaped process is indistinguishable from a revoked one; expiry also performs none of the revocation actions below, so it would leave a credential valid with its census entry gone. Staleness is instead removed by the reconciliation sweep against the spawn snapshot (Spawn event stream, below) on bus-module start and every 60 s thereafter. The sweep reads the bucket, which is why the bus-module grant carries census read as well as write. Growth is bounded by one key per module id with history 1, not by time.
- Invariant: no subject traffic from a participant whose census key is absent. Enforcement point, named because a KV read cannot authorize a NATS publish: the census entry and the participant's credential are one act, so deleting the entry *is* revoking the credential. Revocation is four ordered steps, and the order is chosen so that the server-side refusal is reachable rather than pre-empted by a local failure: (1) read `user_jwt_id` from the census value, add it to the box account's revocation list, and push the updated account claims to the server over the system-account user's claims-update subject, which the directory-backed resolver persists — from this moment the JWT is refused on any new connection and stays refused across a server restart; (2) delete the census key; (3) kick the client over `$SYS` to close the live connection; (4) delete the Claustrum signing record, so no future `credential.sign` for that name succeeds. Steps (1)–(3) are the revocation; step (4) is cleanup whose absence never leaves the JWT usable, and whose presence must not be mistaken for the revocation: with only step (4) done the client fails locally with `Absent` inside `credential.sign` and the server never sees it, which is a different observable from a refused reconnect. A kick alone is not revocation either: it closes a socket and leaves a valid JWT.
- Observables of that sequence, stated so the arm cannot be read two ways. The kick severs the connection, so a publish already in flight may land and the next write on the severed socket surfaces `Unavailable`, not `Denied`. The `$SYS` client-disconnect event carries the kick reason. The client's reconnect presents the revoked JWT and the server refuses it, which the trait layer maps to `Denied` (server "authorization violation"); that refusal must be surfaced within the bound in Constants, and it must be produced by the server rather than by a missing local signing record — which is why step (4) is last. A participant that disables automatic reconnect observes `Unavailable` and nothing further, which is why the arm drives an explicit reconnect.
- Defence in depth, not the enforcement point: the trait layer watches the bucket and fails a publish locally with `Denied` only on a *confirmed* absence — a snapshot received on the current connection that does not contain the key, or an observed delete event for it. A watch that has not yet received a snapshot, or a watch on a dropped connection, is neutral and denies nothing, because otherwise every supervised server restart would make every participant self-deny (Standing rules: absence is neutral). A client bypassing the trait layer gets none of this, which is why the server-side revocation is the one that counts.
- Key lifecycle: on the supervisor's exit event the bus module deletes that module's key and executes revocation; a respawn overwrites the same key at a higher spawn generation with epoch 0, so a crash loop does not grow the bucket. A membership change follows the same re-mint path at the next epoch of the current generation and revokes the superseded epoch by the same four steps. A missed exit event is caught by the reconciliation sweep. The register answers the deployed question (what a running binary understands), which no lock file or `connz` can.

Spawn event stream (owed by SUBC; it does not exist today and must not be polled into existence). Contract required for the census to be recoverable: subscribing returns an atomic snapshot of currently-live (module id, spawn generation, pid) together with the sequence number that snapshot is consistent at, and events replay from any retained sequence. The bus module records the last processed sequence; on restart it resumes there, or takes a fresh snapshot and reconciles — minting for live generations it has no entry for, and revoking plus deleting entries with no live generation. The same reconciliation runs every 60 s against a fresh snapshot, and is what removes entries whose exit event was missed. Generation fencing: a mint request for generation N is refused when the snapshot shows a higher generation for that module, so a stale generation loses authority rather than racing the current one; epochs within the snapshot's current generation are the bus module's own counter and are fenced against the highest pair it has issued, not against the snapshot, because the supervisor never sees a membership re-mint. Acceptance covers a bus-module restart while participants keep running and a respawn during the subscription gap; every current generation ends with exactly one usable census identity.

Tenancy (operator, 2026-09-18) — obligations only; hosted build-out is a non-goal. (a) Every `ck.`-rooted subject, stream name and bucket name contains the account token, subject to the closed exemption list above; a name that does not is a build failure in the naming crate's tests. (b) Every credential-minting record carries an account field; a mint without one is refused. (c) The leaf configuration names exactly one hub, taken from `callosum.hub_read`; a second hub entry is refused. (d) A box with no hub keeps delivering locally under its box account, so a disconnected local deployment is supported and tested. The local `nats-server` is a server on its own box and may additionally run as a leaf of a hub; it is never assumed to be the fleet's only server. The daemon is neither client nor server. The hosted shape is `nats-server` with accounts, the same ceremony with a different issuer, never a second enrollment.

Constants. These are normative defaults; changing one is a spec edit, not a worker choice. Each names the observable that fails when exceeded.
- Minimum versions, because the observables this spec gates on are version-specific (KV history and direct get, pull-consumer API subjects, multi-filter durable consumers, `MaxDeliveriesExceeded` advisory shape, the `$SYS` kick and claims-update requests, directory-backed resolver persistence, leafnode credential handling): `nats-server` 2.10 or later, `async-nats` 0.33 or later. A rig that finds an older server records the skip `nats-server-too-old` with the observed version rather than running and reporting a different behaviour as a failure. The exact minor floors are owed confirmation by SUBC against the version the plane actually ships; until confirmed, arm A9's committed golden is the authority for every version-sensitive subject string.
- Server binary discovery: the rig reads `CK_NATS_SERVER_BIN`, else the first `nats-server` on `PATH`; never an operator-machine absolute path. Absent binary is the recorded skip `nats-server-absent`.
- Connect-path `credential.sign`: deadline 2 s, 3 transient retries, then the connect attempt fails `Unavailable` and enters backoff. A `Clamped` admission delay (below) is not a transient failure and does not consume a retry; the client waits the reported retry-after.
- Reconnect backoff: base 250 ms, factor 2, ceiling 30 s, jitter ±20%. On reaching the ceiling the client emits `bus.link.backoff_ceiling` once per escalation, which is the observable a flapping hub produces (federation #20: bounded so it cannot spend a vault's read limiter on nonce signatures).
- Revocation surfacing bound: a kicked participant that reconnects surfaces `Denied` within 5 s of the kick; exceeding it fails the arm.
- Membership re-mint bound: a room join or leave takes effect — new grant minted at the next credential epoch, census key overwritten at that epoch, client reconnected — within 10 s of the membership write; the arm measures publish refused before and accepted after, and the reverse for a leave. While the bus module is unlanded this bound times the rig fixture's own re-mint and is recorded rather than gated (acceptance_sketch, A9).
- `callosum.hub_read` poll: 60 s. A roster tombstone or identity change disconnects the leaf within 75 s of the roster write; the arm measures that bound.
- Census reconciliation sweep: 60 s. Census bucket: history 1, no TTL.
- Sentinel probe: period 10 s, timeout 2 s, three consecutive failures report `bus.health.down`.
- WorkQueue redelivery cap: 5, then the claiming module's terminal disposition to `ck.{acct}.effect.dead` with `MaxDeliveriesExceeded`.
- Durable workload consumer configuration, shipped and fixture-identical: pull, explicit ack policy, ack wait 30 s, `filter_subjects` carrying one literal entry per bound room or agent in the subset forms above (multi-filter consumers are a 2.10 feature, part of why the floor is 2.10), max-deliver 5 on `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT` and unlimited elsewhere with `nak(delay)` carrying the backoff. A rig consumer whose configuration differs from this fails the arm rather than reporting a pass, so cursor replay and cap exhaustion are measured against the configuration the plane ships.
- Stream limits, so the retention ordering has a comparable value on the broker side. `CK_{ACCT}_ROOM`, `CK_{ACCT}_WAKE`, `CK_{ACCT}_PEER`: max-age 24 h, max-bytes 1 GiB, discard old. `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT` (work queue): max-age 24 h, max-bytes 256 MiB, discard new, and a publish refused for a full queue is reported `Unavailable` with the limit named, never dropped silently. `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD`: max-age 7 d, max-bytes 64 MiB, discard old. Each port slice declares its owning store's retention and the limits crate refuses a configuration where the store's retention is below the stream's max-age; the peer store's current 48 h retention is above the 24 h PEER max-age and is the worked example.
- Cold-start herd: 32 concurrent participants on one box, each paying one `credential.sign` per nonce. Jitter alone bounds nothing — 32 independent draws over 0–2 s exceed 16 in a second often enough to flake a conforming implementation — and a token bucket inside the trait layer bounds nothing either, because 32 supervised processes share no library state and 32 per-process buckets admit 32 simultaneous bursts. The enforcement point is therefore the one process every signer already talks to: a vault-side admission limiter on `credential.sign` for this plane's records, shared across all callers on the box, owed by CKCRED (Credentials, surface item (d)). Its rule is a sliding window and not a token bucket, because at this bound the two are not interchangeable: at most 16 admissions in any 1 s window, evaluated half-open over [t−1 s, t] at the moment of admission. A rate-16/s burst-16 bucket admits 16 signs at t=0 and a seventeenth at t=62.5 ms — 17 inside one window — and would fail the acceptance bound while being otherwise conforming, so the rule is fixed here rather than the nominal rate alone. A sign that would exceed the window is admitted late, never refused, and reported `Clamped` with its retry-after (Standing rules: a reply that clamps reports the clamp); the trait layer's whole obligation is to honour that retry-after rather than spin and to emit `bus.connect.admission_delayed` when it does. The arm drives all 32 requests queued against an injected clock so the window boundary is decided by the limiter's rule rather than by run-to-run timing, and asserts that no 1 s window at the limiter exceeds 16 admissions, that the delay observable fired, and that all 32 participants reach an authenticated publish with none reporting `Unavailable` from the connect-path sign deadline; against the rig-local limiter stand-in it gates the client half only and records `ckcred-admission-limit-unlanded` for the vault half.

Standing rules.
- Absence is neutral: a missing register key, a missing window, a missing reading is reported as absent, never resolved to the granting cause; and an unobserved state — a watch with no snapshot, a dropped connection — is not absence at all.
- A reply that clamps a request reports the clamp (the rooms ack lesson of 2026-09-18).


## acceptance_sketch

Every arm pairs with a control that fails for the intended reason and passes otherwise (room #24: a fixture invalid for an unrelated reason reads as a confident wrong answer without one); this includes the constants and body-resolution arms at the end, which carry their controls inline. Arms run on an empty vault and empty broker store, not only on a pre-provisioned fixture, and every NATS-backed arm runs against a server at or above the minimum version in Constants, discovered by `CK_NATS_SERVER_BIN` or `PATH` and never by an operator absolute path.

External dependencies and disposition. An arm whose prerequisite has not landed does not silently vanish: it runs as a recorded skip carrying the named reason, and the rig fails if a skip is unnamed. Where this repository stands a rig-local fixture in place of an unlanded external component, the arm is labelled with that fixture and gates only the contract the fixture implements; the rig fails — never passes — if an arm reports a result while neither the external component nor its declared fixture was stood up.

Rig provisioning fixture **F-PROV**, declared once here and named in every row that rests on it, because the arms that gate hardest depend on provisioning this repository does not own. F-PROV performs exactly these acts, all under the bus-module-shaped credential it mints for itself:

1. Creates the five streams with the literal subject bindings in constraints and the census bucket.
2. Creates every durable workload consumer the arms pull from, because the per-process grant forbids consumer create on the four workload streams and the bus module that owns this act in production is unlanded. Each is created with the shipped configuration in Constants (pull, explicit ack, ack wait 30 s, max-deliver 5 on `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT`) and with a filter subject that is a subset of its stream's binding: `c_{agent_id}` on `CK_{ACCT}_ROOM` with `filter_subjects` carrying the literal `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.post` once per bound room; `c_{agent_id}` on `CK_{ACCT}_PEER` filtered `ck.{acct}.peer.{agent_id}.*.deliver`; `c_{agent_id}` on `CK_{ACCT}_WAKE` filtered `ck.{acct}.wake.{agent_id}.fire`; `c_{agent_id}` on `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT` filtered `ck.{acct}.effect.{agent_id}.*.intent`; `c_ckbus_dead` on `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD` filtered on the literal `ck.{acct}.effect.dead`. An arm whose consumer configuration differs from this one fails the rig rather than reporting a pass, so cursor replay and cap exhaustion exercise the configuration the plane ships; and a rig run that asks for a `.>` filter reproduces the server's own `JSConsumerFilterNotSubsetErr`, which is the control that the declared filters are the ones a real server accepts.
3. Mints per-process participant credentials at a stated (generation, epoch) bound to named agent and room ids.
4. Writes one census key per credential it mints — key `{module_id}`, value carrying the fields constraints enumerates — before that process's first publish. This is load-bearing rather than tidiness: the trait layer denies a publish locally on a *confirmed* census absence, so a participant publishing against a freshly created, empty census bucket self-denies before the server is ever asked, and an arm that passed in that state would be running against a trait layer with the watch omitted. An arm that publishes under a credential with no census key, and has not declared its watch disabled as a labelled fixture deviation, fails the rig. Control, carried by A4: the identical publish under a credential whose census key F-PROV withheld is denied locally with `Denied` and no server round trip, which proves the watch is live and that the gating arms pass because the key is present and not because the check is absent.
5. Mints the bus-module-shaped credential the stand-in probe runs under, and executes the membership re-mint and reconnect itself at the next epoch.

F-PROV stands in for the bus module's bootstrap, provisioning and re-mint path and depends on CKCRED's mint op, so every arm resting on it records `ckcred-mint-unlanded` rather than passing when that op is absent. An arm that reports any result while F-PROV was not stood up fails the rig.

| Arm | External item | Seat | Disposition when unlanded |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 supervised server lifecycle | `protocol: "none"` mode | SUBC | recorded skip `subc-protocol-none-unlanded` |
| A2 seed absence / child signing | CKCRED mint, delete and audit-read ops; per-process principal at spawn | CKCRED, SUBC | seed half gates on the rig-local signing-record fixture; skips `ckcred-mint-unlanded`, `ckcred-audit-read-unlanded`; child half is a recorded observation, never a gate (constraints, Credentials) |
| A3 census and revocation | bus module + spawn event stream; CKCRED delete; claims-update push | SUBC, CKCRED | recorded skip `bus-module-unlanded`, `spawn-stream-unlanded`, `ckcred-delete-unlanded` |
| A4 stream durability, fanout and re-key | device re-key path; F-PROV (streams, consumers, census keys, bound per-process credentials) | CALLO, CKCRED | cursor and fanout halves gate on F-PROV; re-key half recorded skip `callo-rekey-unlanded`; `ckcred-mint-unlanded` when F-PROV cannot mint |
| A5 trust and link | roster column, hello field, `callosum.hub_read`, leaf signing shape, leaf credential | CALLO, SUBC | recorded skip per missing item, including `bus-module-unlanded` for the leaf credential; link arm labelled with its leaf-signing shape |
| A6 trait conformance | none | — | gates |
| A7 no regression | none | — | gates |
| A8 sentinel probe | probe host (bus module); F-PROV (streams, census bucket and key, bus-module-shaped credential) | SUBC, CKCRED | gates against a rig-hosted stand-in probe implementing the probe contract in constraints; skip `ckcred-mint-unlanded` when F-PROV cannot mint; the module-hosted run is a recorded observation carrying `bus-module-unlanded` |
| A9 grant conformance on a live server | bus-module and system-account users; install bootstrap; F-PROV including consumers and the rig-executed membership re-mint | CKCRED, SUBC | gates with the rig minting those two users and the two account JWTs itself as declared fixtures; recorded skip `ckcred-mint-unlanded` when the mint op is absent, plus `nats-server-absent` / `nats-server-too-old`; the committed golden below stays authoritative through any skip |

A1. A local `nats-server` runs under subc in the declared non-subc mode: `ck` shows it present with `live` not-applicable; on a supervisor restart `ck module terminals nats` records `exit_signal` SIGTERM with a clean exit status and the restart completes in under a second. Control: the same restart with the declaration removed records SIGKILL after the drain ceiling, where the expected ceiling is read from the supervisor's declared configuration at run time and never hard-coded. Store intactness is not the discriminator (a write-ahead log survives SIGKILL too) and a missing log line is not evidence.

A2. Seed absence, on enumerated surfaces only: `/proc/<pid>/environ`, the process argv, and the module's own config and state directories contain no string matching the nkey seed form `S[UAOCN][A-Z2-7]{54}`. Stated with the arm: a negative over an unbounded surface is not a proof, so this arm claims absence on those surfaces and nothing more. The gating half does not wait on the bus module, but it does wait on CKCRED's mint and audit-read ops (constraints, Credentials): the rig mints the signing record `nats.{module_id}.g{generation}.e{epoch}` in Claustrum itself, under the same name grammar and the same per-process grant the bus module would use, and the arm says it is running against that fixture; if the mint op is absent the arm is the recorded skip `ckcred-mint-unlanded` rather than a pass. The module then authenticates by a `credential.sign` call for that credential name, read from Claustrum's audit log by the record-name and caller-principal fields, or skipped as `ckcred-audit-read-unlanded` if that read surface does not exist. Child observation (not a gate): a child spawned by that authenticating module, given the credential name and the public JWT, attempts `route.open` plus `credential.sign` over the ordinary local route; the result is recorded either way, because the evidence shows the inherited launch-nonce principal carries that sign authority today (constraints). Control: the parent performs the same call and succeeds, so a failure of the child arm is not a failure of the route.

A3. The census register `CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS` holds exactly one key per live module process, written by the bus module before that process's first subject publish; the value names the process credential public, its `user_jwt_id`, spawn generation, credential epoch and bound rooms. A respawn overwrites the same key at a higher generation with epoch 0 and revokes the prior credential; a membership re-mint overwrites it at the same generation and the next epoch.

Revocation arm, following the four ordered steps in constraints and their distinct observables. The bus module reads `user_jwt_id` from the census value, pushes it into the box account claims and lets the resolver persist it, deletes the census key, kicks the client over `$SYS`, and only then deletes the Claustrum signing record. Observed: the next write on the severed connection surfaces `Unavailable`; the `$SYS` client-disconnect event carries the kick reason; the client's explicit reconnect with the revoked JWT is refused *by the server* — the arm asserts the server-side authorization error, not merely a failed connect — and the trait layer reports `Denied` within 5 s of the kick. A second reconnect after a server restart is still refused, which is what separates revocation from a socket close and what proves the claims update was persisted rather than held in memory. Controls, each isolating one step: an unkicked participant with a present key publishes and reconnects successfully; a participant whose trait-layer watch is disabled is severed and refused on reconnect just the same, proving the server and not the client is the enforcement point; a participant kicked without the claims update reconnects successfully, which is the control that would pass if the spec had treated the kick as the revocation; a participant for whom *only* the signing record was deleted fails locally with `Absent` inside `credential.sign` and is never seen by the server, which is the control that distinguishes client-side breakage from server-side refusal; and a bus-module credential regenerated without census read fails step (1) outright — it cannot read the JWT id — rather than silently revoking nothing, which is the control that proves the read grant is load-bearing.

Recovery arm: the bus module restarts while participants keep running, and a participant respawns during the subscription gap; afterwards every live generation has exactly one usable census identity and every stale (generation, epoch) pair is refused. Longevity arm: with the sweep clock driven by an injected time source, a participant alive across several sweep periods keeps its key and publishes throughout — no expiry path reaps a live process — while an entry whose process exited without an exit event is removed by the first sweep after the snapshot shows it gone, with its credential revoked by the same ordered steps. The sweep reads every key under the bus-module grant; a sweep that cannot list the bucket fails the arm rather than reporting a clean reconciliation.

A4. Fanout, cursor durability and re-key on the streams and consumers F-PROV created, each on the stream whose subject shape actually supports it, and all under generated production grants rather than an unrestricted fixture — the publishing identities are bound to the room under test at mint time, and each carries the census key F-PROV wrote, so the arm exercises the room grant lifecycle rather than bypassing it. Fanout: one publish on `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.post` reaches durable consumers `c_{agent_id}` on two registry identities, both filtered on the literal `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.post` — the subset form the ROOM binding accepts — while peer subjects carry exactly one agent id and two peer filters are disjoint, so fanout is not testable there and is not claimed there. Cursor durability: on `CK_{ACCT}_PEER`, a consumer `c_{agent_id}` filtered on its own `ck.{acct}.peer.{agent_id}.*.deliver` replays from its stored cursor after a module restart. Re-key arm: the same device's Ed25519 companion key is rotated through CALLO's ceremony re-key path with the registry identity id unchanged and the roster row revision incremented — distinguished from delete-and-recreate by that unchanged id — and both cursors and both consumer names survive. Controls: delete-and-recreate of the identity does orphan the consumer, which is the behaviour the re-key must not exhibit; and the census-watch control named with F-PROV — the same publish under a credential whose census key was withheld is denied locally, before the server, which proves these passes rest on a present key and not on an absent check.

A5. Trust arms on the two-daemon rig (two daemons, one box, separate XDG homes): pairing writes the hub column with the hub's TLS SPKI SHA-256; the leaf pins it; the leaf refuses a hub that presents a valid WebPKI-or-self-signed TLS chain and valid credentials but a different SPKI; a tombstoned hub row disconnects the leaf within 75 s of the roster write. Link arm on a containerised NAT rig (leaf egress only, hub listener reachable, inbound to the leaf blocked): a message published on the hub reaches a consumer on the leaf over the per-host credential, while an inbound dial to the leaf fails — this is the gating arm, and it is labelled with the leaf-signing shape it ran under. The Hetzner-as-hub with this Mac as leaf run is a recorded manual observation with date and host, never a gate. Mac-as-hub is untestable from this desk and is stated as such, not left open.

A6. The trait layer executes the conformance suite as an enumerated property list, each property marked parity or NATS-only per the constraints table: parity properties run on both backends and must agree; NATS-only properties (restart-durable cursor, re-key-durable cursor, server-enforced denial, reconnect refusal after revocation, leaf behaviour, `$SYS` events) run only on the NATS backend and are reported as not-applicable for in-memory, never as passes. Control: a deliberately weakened NATS implementation fails the NATS-only set while still passing parity, proving the suite is not satisfiable by parity alone. Included parity properties: publish ack sequence, replay from cursor, register revision and absent-vs-empty, watch snapshot-then-updates and whether a snapshot has been received on this connection, work redelivery count, cap exhaustion to `ck.{acct}.effect.dead` with `MaxDeliveriesExceeded` and its dead-letter record, a publish refused by a work queue at its configured max-bytes reported `Unavailable` with the exhausted limit named on both backends, and the `Unavailable`/`Denied`/`Absent`/`Clamped` taxonomy including the connection-boundary mapping rule, the sentinel class-attribution rule (a permissions violation observed on the connection's async-error surface outranks a requester timeout), and the rule that a sign against a deleted record is `Absent` and never `Denied`.

A7. Nothing in prefrontal's delivery paths changes in this cut. The existing offline rig under `tests/docker/` (harness, daemon, store, wire, restart) stays green, and recorded request/response transcripts for `agent_delivery`, `wake_fire`, `effect_intent` and the Pi plugin-session push are compared against committed goldens under a declared normalization envelope, because those records carry values that differ on every run.

The envelope is committed and closed, and it is enumerated **per transcript**, because the four transcripts carry different identifier families and one global list hid three of them. Each transcript's recording declares, for every identifier-bearing field it emits, either the derivation that makes it deterministic or its membership in that transcript's envelope; a field in neither list fails the recording. Shared across all four: `due_at`, `created_at`, `delivered_at`, `next_reconcile_at`, `reconcile_deadline`, `intent_epoch`, `connection_epoch`, and the counter-derived `delivery-{n}` ids. Content digests are *not* substituted: `delivered_payload_hash` is content-derived — `docs/specs/wakes.md:76` makes the digest the payload hash and `crates/prefrontal-core-store/migrations/082_wake_delivery.sql:120-125` constrains it to 64 lowercase hex — so normalizing it would let a payload change that alters only the digest compare equal. It belongs in each transcript's derivation list, and enters that transcript's envelope only when the recording names the specific nondeterministic input (a timestamp composed into the body, say) that makes it irreproducible, with that input recorded next to the field. `wake_fire` adds `fire_id` (`wf_` plus 16 hex, `crates/prefrontal-core-store/migrations/082_wake_delivery.sql:103-125`) and the effect id derived from the sorted fire ids (`docs/specs/wakes.md:76`), which is deterministic only relative to the fire ids and is therefore normalized with them. `effect_intent` adds `owner_provider` and `process_instance_id`, minted per plugin boot (`crates/prefrontal-core-store/migrations/006_effects.sql:12-38`). `agent_delivery` adds the peer message id and `claim_id`. The plugin-session push adds `registration_id` and `session_id`. Whether any of these is content-derived rather than random is not settled by this package, so the recording slice settles it per field and records the answer next to the field. Each substituted value takes a fixed placeholder applied identically to golden and observed; every other byte compares raw, and "byte-for-byte" means that comparison and nothing looser. Goldens are recorded by `tests/docker/record_goldens.sh` against the same rig, and the rig asserts each transcript's envelope has exactly its committed length so no list can be widened to make a failure disappear. Controls: an intentional one-field change outside the envelope fails the comparison; a changed value inside the envelope does not; and — the control that proves the lists are complete rather than merely plausible — two consecutive recordings of the same scenario differ nowhere outside their envelopes, which fails today for any identifier family left unenumerated.

A8. Sentinel probe, gating against the rig-hosted stand-in that implements the probe contract in constraints (requester and responder in one process, replying through the server) under the bus-module-shaped credential F-PROV mints, with its census key present. With the server running, the probe reports `bus.health.up` within two periods, and the reply is observed arriving on `_INBOX.{credential_public}.*` under the generated grant, so the arm proves the round trip rather than a publish. Server stopped: three consecutive failures report `bus.health.down` with class `Unavailable`; server restarted, the first success reports `bus.health.up`. Cold start with the probe running before the server has ever listened reports `bus.health.down`, never healthy-from-silence. A run against the real bus-module-hosted probe is recorded as an observation carrying `bus-module-unlanded` until that module exists. Controls: a probe whose reply subject is misrouted still reports down rather than up; a probe whose grant is regenerated without publish on `_INBOX.{credential_public}.>` reports down with class `Denied` while the server is healthy — the class is attributed from the connection's async-error surface under the attribution rule in constraints, because the requester's own observable in that scenario is a reply timeout and `async-nats` surfaces the responder's permissions violation asynchronously rather than as a return from `publish`, and the paired observation that separates the two classes is the server-stopped run above reporting `Unavailable` with reply publish permitted; and a probe whose client leaves the library-default random inbox prefix *connects successfully*, is refused server-side when it subscribes to that default reply subject, and reports down — the arm asserts the subscribe-time permissions violation and never a connect failure, because a correct server accepts that connection and an arm expecting otherwise would fail a conforming implementation.

A9. Grant conformance against a running server, which is the arm that settles every permission string this spec cannot settle from documentation. The rig mints the box-local operator key, the two account JWTs, the bus-module user and the system-account user itself, as declared fixtures alongside F-PROV, and runs from an empty vault with no fleet operator key present anywhere. Under the per-process grant: a pull on its own consumer succeeds — that consumer was created by F-PROV under the management credential, never by the participant, whose own create attempt is in the refused list below; an ack on each of its own literal ack subjects `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_ROOM.c_{agent_id}.>`, `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_WAKE.c_{agent_id}.>`, `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_PEER.c_{agent_id}.>`, `$JS.ACK.CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT.c_{agent_id}.>` succeeds — the arm never exercises a partial-token form; a census get succeeds, and a census watch succeeds *including* the ordered-consumer create and delete it issues under `KV_CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS`, which the per-process grant authorizes there and nowhere else; a publish to `ck.{acct}.effect.dead` succeeds; a publish to `ck.{acct}.room.{room_id}.post` for a bound room succeeds. Refused, each observed as a server-side `Denied`: an ack published on another identity's ack subject; a pull or consumer INFO on another identity's consumer; a consumer create on any of the four workload streams `CK_{ACCT}_{ROOM|WAKE|PEER|EFFECT}`; a write to `$KV.CK_{ACCT}_CENSUS.>`; a publish to `ck.{acct}.room.{other_room_id}.post` for a room the identity is not bound to; any `$SYS` subject; any sentinel subject. Under the bus-module grant: census get, watch, put and delete all succeed — the read half is exercised, not assumed, because the reconciliation sweep and revocation step (1) rest on it; stream and consumer management on all five literal stream names succeeds, including creating the durable workload consumers with the declared filter subjects and configuration, and including `CK_{ACCT}_EFFECT_DEAD` with its `c_ckbus_dead` consumer; sentinel publish, sentinel subscribe and the reply publish on its own `_INBOX.{credential_public}.>` all succeed; and a workload publish is refused. Under the system-account user: the kick request, the account claims-update request and the client-connect/disconnect subscriptions succeed, and a workload publish is refused.

Membership lifecycle sub-arm, split so that what gates is implementation-facing. Gating half: F-PROV performs a membership write and re-mints at the next credential epoch of the same spawn generation; the re-minted credential publishes to the newly joined room and is refused server-side (`Denied`) on the departed one, the superseded epoch is refused on reconnect, and the spawn snapshot still reports the original generation throughout — so the arm fails under any implementation that bumps the spawn generation to rotate a credential, and fails under any implementation whose record name collides with the one the next real respawn needs. Fixture-measured half, not a gate: the 10 s membership re-mint bound in Constants times F-PROV's own re-mint and reconnect, so it would pass under a bus module that never re-mints at all; it is recorded with `bus-module-unlanded` and becomes a gate when the bus module owns that path.

A9's output is a build gate that must keep working on machines where A9 cannot run. The subject set the arm exercises is committed to this repository as the permission golden at `tests/grants/permission_golden.txt` — including the claims-update and kick subject strings, which this spec deliberately does not assert from documentation. The generator's inputs for that file are pinned literals rather than the recording host's identity, because a golden regenerated from the local host id would compare equal to itself on every machine and gate nothing: account token `box_goldenfixture` (inside the account lexicon), module id `ckbus`, agent ids `agent_gold_a` and `agent_gold_b`, room ids `room_gold_bound` and `room_gold_unbound` with only the first bound, so the refusal rows for an unbound room and a foreign identity are present in the committed file. The permission generator's own build test feeds exactly those literals and compares its emission against the committed file unconditionally, on every machine, with no server and no vault, so the gate is neither vacuous nor host-dependent. When A9 runs it mints its fixtures under those same literals, regenerates the set and diffs it against the committed golden, failing on any difference; when A9 skips it records the skip and the committed golden remains authoritative. No change to the committed golden lands without an A9 run recorded in the same change: a golden edited while A9 skipped is precisely the failure this rule exists to prevent.
